title: Welcome to the Moving Science Blog
text:
What’s special about that blog? Honestly, I do not know yet! Maybe nothing, except that written blogs run out of fashion. I expect nobody to read it. This reduces the pressure immensely! The old joke is that if you are looking for a safe place to store money, put it in your thesis at the library. It will be there in times of need.
I hope to store some thoughts here and discover what happens to them when they are exposed to the virtual world. Maybe an AI system will pick them up, and my mind will reincarnate in silicon form a couple of decades from now. Maybe some posts reach other biological minds, leading to interesting conversations and discussions. Maybe this blog stays there for a couple of months and vanishes in the vastness of cyberspace. I do not feel confident about any of these predictions. But I am sure my future self will find a nice story about that blog and why it turned out the way it did…

title: Welcome to the Moving Science Blog
text:
What can you expect?
I will mostly write about the science of exercise and human movement related to health. I also have strong interests in psychology and statistics, but that doesn’t mean I am an expert in any of them.
Some posts will be of practical nature and deal with physical exercise, rehabilitation or athletic training. Others might be more theoretical or philosophical at times. In any case, I will try to back up my ideas with scientific theories and my readings of the current literature. I will do as I was taught and cite the origin of thoughts as well as possible (until no original thought can be thought anymore).

title: Welcome to the Moving Science Blog
section: Why do I write this blog?
text:
Why do I write this blog?
Pure scholarship! Allan Watts was talking about studying as leisure and how scholarship contradicts itself when playfulness is not invited (Watts 1995). It’s hard to grasp, but I am trying to follow this principle. The blog is a way to try out ideas - let them express themselves and then rest and sink1. It seems like low risk and low cost compared to writing a book or a paper. Not writing (or not making it public) would rob me of the whole experience. The intention to publish it makes one think harder and care about the writing.
So, I wish myself fun, and I am happy to share it

title: The Non-functionality of Exercise
text:
Terminology of training
In the early 2000s, the term “Functional Training” was in widespread use. The pioneers who brought functional training to the broader community (most notably Gray Cook, Mike Boyle, Greg Glassman, and Mark Verstegen) built a conceptual framework for movement practices to serve human movement effectiveness and efficiency. While their approaches differed from each other, their overarching idea was to build a training concept with broad transfer by implementing movements based on tasks or patterns that recur frequently in sports or daily life. Many of their ideas are built around neurology, motor control, and development from the 1960s onward. Most importantly, they broke with the convention at the time to dissect the human body into single muscles or organ systems. But early on, the Functional Training proponents faced criticism (e.g., Ide et al. 2021; Dominski et al. 2022; Siff 2002). Especially the name angered many coaches and scientists alike. The argument is that the term “Functional” implies that other forms of training are non-functional. This criticism of “Functional” Training is valid, but I think that the term is as good as many other descriptions of exercise programs we use. Oftentimes, we name a training methodology after its intended outcome. The WHY of Functional Training is to gain specific functions. A more precise way of talking about a training method is to talk about the WHAT. To give another example, strength training would be the WHY, while calling it resistance training defines WHAT you do. Making this distinction would open the door for a shift in our attention around movement.



Outcome Goals - the WHY
The language we use when talking about exercise and training is important. It drives our attention and intention around what we do. We use WHY terms to invoke motivation in athletes and the general population. From a public health perspective, talking about strength training could make a lot of sense, as the quality and quantity of the skeletal muscle system is a highly relevant metric when it comes to mortality and quality of life in the elderly and patients. The whole language around exercise and training is built around the notion of goals. They represent the WHY.
Here we come back to the term “functional training.” The dichotomy between functional and non-functional training implies that we know every WHY (i.e., function) that the training has. As I describe in another post, this is even part of the definition of training. The goal lets us focus our attention. However, focus also means that we lose the ability to explore.


Movement practice
By setting goals and calling out the desired outcomes of a training program, we define the meaning of the movement based on future outcomes. An alternative is to let the meaning emerge. The movement only defines the search space, and the interaction with the person creates individual meaning. Instead of a narrow, hard focus, we stay curious, open, and exploratory.
Movement does not have to be functional to be meaningful! It cannot serve a specific goal in itself. The goal can only be revealed by the person and in a certain situation. The outcomes it has on our lives cannot be predicted and shouldn’t be. This is for sure not an alternative to “Training” - it is an expansion.
I want to finish this off with a saying Peter Drucker is frequently credited for (see this post by Danny Buerkli):
“What gets measured gets managed.”
I think in a sense it is still true, but in reverse: You will often try to manage what you measure. But this also means that you will not even recognize the hidden potential in things you do not measure. A movement practice is a way of opening up to the potential of change we cannot foresee. It’s a way to embrace meaning by not installing a predefined purpose.





References

Dominski, Fábio Hech, Ramires Alsamir Tibana, and Alexandro Andrade. 2022. “‘Functional Fitness Training,’ CrossFit, HIMT, or HIFT: What Is the Preferable Terminology?” Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 4.


Ide, Bernardo N., Amanda P. Silvatti, Moacir Marocolo, et al. 2021. “Is There Any Non-functional Training? A Conceptual Review.” Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 3 (January): 803366. https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.803366.


Siff, Mel C. 2002. “Functional Training Revisited.” Strength & Conditioning Journal 24 (5): 42.

title: Intervene When Necessary - Not When Bored
text:
Coaches regularly introduce fancy exercise variations or new complex programs, even when there is no objective reason to do so. If the old program works well and produces results, why change?
Often, we feel the need to further optimize. A program is never perfect, and there is this one particular exercise that would fit so well… Trust me, I feel you!
However, this optimization may just mask the Bored Specialist. Our client gets told how to squat maybe once or twice a week, but the coach may teach that exact squat ten times a day. To “spice it up,” we may implement new variations. But for whom? For us or for them?
The key is to audit ourselves honestly on three levels:

Is it for the athlete? There may be physiological (e.g., stagnation or injuries), psychological (e.g., motivation or monotony), or environmental (e.g., equipment availability) reasons to change the plan. If there are not, stick to it!
Is it for my ego? As coaches, we may feel bored, we want to feel respected and in full control. None of these are reasons for changing the program. But it is still valuable information to you! If you are bored, that is okay. Look at other aspects of your (professional) life you may want to change. Just make sure to check in with your coaching values so you don’t confuse your personal needs with your clients’ needs.
Is it for job security? Quite frequently, I hear coaches express their fears of being dispensable. They try to overcome that through innovation and entertrainment rather than real coaching. But remember that at the core of good coaching is relationship and trust, not information exchange or entertainment.

Try to answer those questions as honestly as possible. Frequently, not intervening is the best we can do. It means overcoming boredom, insecurity, and pride, and being a coach for the athlete, patient, or client in front of you.

title: An Experiment on Attention
text:
In previous posts, I describe the difference between Training and Movement Practice. The goal of training is to drive very specific adaptations with as much input as necessary but as little as possible. Training is an efficiency game. Movement practices are less goal-directed and more experience-oriented. They are not driven by efficiency. The difference comes down to the intention of each session and the overall process.
This post dives into attention during human movement. First, I discuss a connection between dual-processing theory and top-down motor control. Then I lay out a movement practice to explore shifting attention. It is based on willingly switching between internal and external focus of attention 1. I like the presented practice because of its simplicity. It can help break up patterns and find new ways to engage with movement.

title: An Experiment on Attention
section: Attention drives Movement - Movement drives Attention
text:
Attention drives Movement - Movement drives Attention
When I think of human movement, my intuition is to think of manipulating the relationship between the body, or its segments, and the environment. But this is only a small fraction of human movement. Human movement is a broad spectrum of changes in shape and position. It ranges from the microscopic folding of proteins, contraction of blood vessels, and the expansion of the lungs to whole-body rearrangements in space.
Movement is purposeful when it all serves the system’s goals - like preserving life - but there are also random elements to it (Rosenblueth et al. 1943).  There are qualia to many, but not all of our movements. Some internal states are closed to conscious experience or allegedly only available to the most experienced yogis. Most experientially accessible movements have a bidirectional relation with attention. The purpose and intention of movement direct attention. Solutions emerge through this interplay. Attention is active and causal to action. At the same time, attention can be passive when it is affected by movement and its sensory feedback (Fernandez-Duque and Johnson 2002).
Organization of movement is based on multiple parallel and serial processes. One of these processes is based on purpose- and intention-based attention. But its activity use depends on the situation. As popularized by Daniel Kahneman, Dual-processing theories distinguish between System 1 (“thinking fast”) and System 2 (“thinking slow”), (2012) 2. According to this theory, there are two modes or systems of cognition. System 1 is the fast, intuitive, automatic mode. Under System 1, action is built on heuristics and learned associations. System 2 is the slow mode of argumentation and logic. System 2 is not error-free or morally “better”, but it helps break up patterns and find new solutions, in case our typical responses don’t work. Dividing cognition into two distinct systems is a strong simplification (Evans and Stanovich 2013), but it’s useful in describing decisions. Samuel et al. (2026) apply this framework to a broad range of psychological “adaptations”3. Here I will specifically apply it to movement solutions in space.
If the task is hard, the mover is under time pressure or high (cognitive) load, System 1 kicks into full gear and it involves a focus on the external effect of the movement. This is called external focus of attention (Schmidt et al. 2019).
System 2 is only available if there are enough resources available. In our context, this may be possible during reflection, explicit coaching, or trying to cognitively solve a movement puzzle, as well as under low-stakes or slow movements. This is the “slow” top-down mode, which comes with the freedom of willingly directing attention. Under System 2, one can place attention on internal processes of the body (as well as on cognition and emotion). During this internal focus of attention, the mover can be focusing on the knee angle, contractions of the working muscle, or their heartbeat. It is about the feedback from the body or the effects on it.
The two types of focus have been studied for decades now, and most scientists agree that when it comes to learning and performance, an external focus should be preferred (Chua et al. 2021). So if one has the goal of learning or teaching a motor skill, attention should be brought to the external effects of the movement. Typically, this may be the default (system 1) path anyway. But under the control of System 2, some movers start worrying a lot about internal processes.
Internal focus of attention has its place. Many embodied practices (mind-body practices) like yoga, traditional martial arts, and some contemporary dancing schools use internal cues in their teachings. The modern mindfulness trend has a strong emphasis on internal processes, and some applied philosophies use internal focus to train right attention or get a better understanding of reality. By placing attention on the internal feedback of the body, one can improve their understanding of bodily sensations. Some theories describe emotions as interpretations of bodily sensations coupled with environmental cues (Craig 2003; Damasio 2004). Embodied practices could, therefore, support behavioral changes by improved processing and awareness of emotions and feelings.

title: An Experiment on Attention
text:
Attention Practice - Let’s get Esoteric
This post is not just about the scientific, exoteric promises of the practice. It’s about raising curiosity about what is happening to you personally during the proposed practice. It is an esoteric practice, which means that it is research on one’s own internal reality 4. The explicit knowledge about what it should be like is not of interest. It is about your participatory knowing of what is.
The proposed practice is an invitation to be playful but serious. Try it out at least twice while staying open-minded and without grasping for a specific effect.

title: An Experiment on Attention
text:
The practice - A guide
Before starting, make sure to warm up properly and prepare your space and equipment. Turn off your phone or set it aside completely. Prepare your water upfront, if you need that. Everything should be set and ready with minimal external distractions.
Use one or two physical exercises or movement patterns you already know well. You can adapt the practice as you like. At the beginning, I would suggest using equipment like weights or balls because it makes the intended switch of attention much easier. I trained with kettlebells for a while and still use them for this kind of practice. I alternate between presses and rows. But that is a personal choice. Look for a challenging weight that you can move about 8 to 20 times with good form. You will do about three to six sets of each exercise without ever going to failure.
Set a timer that signals the start of each new set, so you focus on the actual practice. Try 60 to 180-second intervals, depending on the relative load and the movement. For starters: the heavier the implement, the longer the rest time. There is no need for more details here. Once everything is set up, you can start the practice. Every time the signal goes off, start your set. In between sets, walk a bit or just sit down. So far, it might not be so different from your typical exercise session, but here comes the essential part:
Whenever you do your exercise, your focus should be very narrow and specific. Imagen moving your implement towards or away from something. For example, while lifting an object, you can focus on getting it away from the ground as fast and forcefully as possible. Similarly, you could focus on pressing the implement up towards the ceiling or moving it away from your shirt. Use an external focus and a clear intention that can be expressed in an image (“forceful”, “powerful”, “like a crane”, “like a rocket”, “rip it off the floor”, “throw it far away”…). The moment you finish the exercise, you flip a switch and bring your attention to your bodily sensations. Notice how long it takes for your muscles to “turn off”, how your blood pressure drops, and how breathing regulates. Stay open to whatever rises to consciousness. There are thousands of regulatory processes going on, and some of them are observable if you are curious and open. When the signal goes off again, repeat that cycle. That’s it.

title: An Experiment on Attention
text:
Further recommendations
I recommend a warm up before practice. Nevertheless, this does not mean you have to be optimally prepared. It may be interesting to play around with your arousal and your level of fatigue. Just be warmed up sufficiently to feel safe with the exercise you choose.
Keep the practice as simple as possible and try it out multiple times. Maybe you can embrace the simplicity. If you feel bored during the session, stay with the boredom. It is fine. Just flip a switch during the next set and focus on the performance during the lift. Then boredom might arise again or not. Both are fine.
Later, you can play around with the exercise selection by using bodyweight exercises, stretching, or even everyday movements like making coffee. You can play around with more challenging environments, too. For now, you might stick to my initial recommendations - equipment to move, medium intensity, and minimal external distractions.
You can turn the whole concept on its head. Switch to an internal focus of attention during the set, and bring your attention to your exteroceptive input (like sight and sounds) during rest. I typically use a broader, more open awareness to contrast with the set’s narrow focus.
For comparison, a similar idea is Joseph Bartz’s Low Sugar Training. He makes it even more raw. But I personally think that some extra instructions help. If you have ever experimented with dance or musical improvisations, you may know by heart how hard it is to move freely without any guidance or boundaries.

title: An Experiment on Attention
text:
Summary of the practice

Find a distraction-free environment.
Warm up appropriately.
Decide on one or two exercises. Use exercises you have some experience with, and use moderately heavy weights.
Set an interval timer to 60-180 seconds for 3-6 sets.
Every time the alarm goes off, you do a set of the exercise without going to failure. Leave about 1-3 reps in the tank.
During the set, your full attention is focused on an external goal of the movement.
You switch to the internal sensations the moment you put down the implement and stick with it throughout the rest period.
Do not add anything to the practice before trying it out at least two to three times.
Embrace simplicity and use your curiosity without leaning into any expectations about what the practice will yield.
Enjoy!

title: An Experiment on Attention
text:
Footnotes


In motor learning literature, it is common to call it internal and external “focus of attention”. But this is somewhat imprecise, and some fields distinguish clearly between attention and focus. Attention can be described as the process of directing your mental processes towards something, while focus is the sustained (more narrow) attention on something.↩︎
Some authors reject the term system and prefer dual types or dual processes (Evans and Stanovich 2013)↩︎
Their use of the word adaptations overlaps partly with mine, but is not fully congruent.↩︎
The word esoteric has many different meanings. Originally it was used as a differentiation from exoteric philosophies and it means something like “secret” or “inner” philosophy. Coming from a time when philosophy and science were two sides of the same coin, esoteric can mean something like the knowledge (or wisdom) that reveals itself only to the experts or the knowledge (or wisdom) that is only attainable through insight into ones’ own nature of reality.↩︎

title: About
text:
Dear reader,
This blog is my effort to make sense of everything related to exercise science, human movement, and psychology. It is said that many great scientist answered in a similar way when asked about the practical implications of their findings:
We don’t do it because it is important - We do it because it is interesting.
This blog is mainly a personal experiment. (No, I do not need a hypothesis for that.) Feel free to leave comments or send me a message. No likes or subscriptions needed.
Peter Raidl

title: Exercise Program by AI
text:
At the beginning of each semester, I ask students what they expect learning in the seminar Training Processes that I teach at the University of Vienna. The answer I hear most often is that they want to be able to write a good exercise program. At that point in their education, they have already learned the foundations of exercise physiology, biomechanics, and training science. They know the basic training principles, prioritization structures, and recommendations for a specific adaptation. Nevertheless, they do not feel competent writing a training plan for athletes.
Then, we let LLMs write an exercise program for their hypothetical athlete, and they reflect on the output. Can your favorite large language model plan your training for *pick your goal and athlete*? The simple answer to that is yes! For many people and common goals, AI is doing a great job writing a training structure. It is doing a better job than 80% of human coaches. Sure, there are concerns with this approach. The LLMs do not really “know” training science. They predict words based on their training data, which can sometimes lead to serious hallucinations. They have problems with numbers, and simple repetition recommendations are occasionally off. Otherwise, LLMs are doing great.
But this shouldn’t even surprise us! There is so much information on the internet about how to run a marathon or train for a bigger bench press. Even before AI and social media, writing a basic exercise program was relatively easy- especially for beginners or some specific populations. You could open any book on training and find a good structure. So don’t be surprised if AI is as good as your next best coach!
Interestingly, the students can easily fact-check the AI. They can immediately see the major issues with the outlined training structure and correct them. But it is also a mindboggling experience. They want to learn something that the current LLMs already can do well1.


From a coaching perspective, I differentiate the training process into five phases. Each phase has its purpose and order. Naturally, this is just a rough guideline. The order is not fixed, and an experienced coach often jumps between phases. Writing the exercise program is just a tiny part of the process, which I call “drawing the map”. If you have a map, you are ahead of the game - But only if you have a clear destination, know what you are capable of, and can navigate and adjust if the road is blocked.



Coaching steps during the training process


Therefore, the more interesting question is, can AI do all that? The only way training can work out long-term is when regular adjustments happen according to the physiological and psychological needs of the person in relation to the goals and environmental constraints given. I am definitely not saying that AI can not do that. But this is the Training Science Turing Test we should think about. It is not interesting if it can write down 10 exercises in the correct order and the right repetition zones according to all the books published about training.

title: From the Archive: Das eigene Weltbild zum Einsturz bringen
text:
Jene Person, welche die eigene Meinung nach der Lektüre eines einzelnen wissenschaftlichen Artikels um 180 Grad dreht, hat wahrscheinlich einfach noch wenig Wissen und Erfahrung zum entsprechenden Thema. Andererseits gibt es die Gefahr, am eigenen Weltbild hängen zu bleiben und alle Gegenargumente gekonnt abzuwenden. Damit das nicht passiert, ist es hilfreich von Zeit zu Zeit eine Metaperspektive einzunehmen.

Identität und Weltbild
Das Ideal einer rein objektiven Wissenschaft bleibt ein unerreichbares Ziel. Gerade in Bereichen, in denen neben biologisch beschreibbaren auch mentalen Prozesse eine erhebliche Rolle spielen, ist Objektivität erschwert. Mentale Prozesse haben zwar eine biologische Grundlage, aber diese sind nur rückschlüssig interpretierbar.
Das bedeutet gleichzeitig nicht, das Ideal einer empirischen Wissenschaft ad acta zu legen: Gute Forscher*innen reflektieren ihre unabdingbare Subjektivität und bewahren ihre Integrität. Aber das ist nicht immer so einfach. Der Druck, richtig zu liegen und echtes Wissen zu mehren, ist hoch. Dürfen Praktiker*innen und Forscher*innen irren? Wenn nicht, ist die Verteidigung der eigenen Forschung keine wissenschaftliche Angelegenheit mehr, sondern das Verteidigen des eigenen Egos und des sozialen Status. Von einem (erfahrungs-)offenen Geist kann nicht mehr gesprochen werden. Dieses Thema geht uns alle an. Sobald politische oder wissenschaftliche Positionen für die eigene Identität instrumentalisiert werden, ist es fast unmöglich eine Metaperspektive zu entwickeln, die uns für die subjektive Erfahrung öffnet.
Identifiziert sich eine Person sehr stark mit ihrem konkreten Weltbild, dient das Weltbild nicht mehr als Instrument, das auch mal überprüft werden muss, sondern als Klebstoff für die eigene Persönlichkeit.
Das Weltbild muss erhalten bleiben, damit eine Person im Gleichgewicht bleibt. Die Folge: Die Welt wird ausschließlich assimiliert, d.h. Erfahrungsinhalte werden in das bestehende Wissen eingefügt. Akkommodation, d.h. die Veränderung mentaler Prozesse aufgrund von Erfahrungsinhalten findet kaum mehr statt.
Der Grund für dieses Phänomen ist keine charakterliche Schwäche des Individuums. Erfahrungsinhalte, die sich von der eigenen Weltsicht derart unterscheiden, dass sie nicht assimiliert werden können, werden schlicht nicht oder nur in geringem Maße wahrgenommen. Erfahrungsinhalte, die in das Weltbild passen, werden andererseits aktiv mit Bedeutung aufgeladen.


They Saw a Game
Einer der klassischsten Texte zu diesem Phänomen ist die Studie „They Saw a Game“ von Albert Hastorf und Hadley Cantril von 1952 (Link). Ein Text, den wir nicht nur aufgrund seiner wissenschaftsgeschichtlichen Bedeutung sehr empfehlen. Die Untersuchung befasst sich mit der Wahrnehmung eines Footballspiels, welches das Team der Universität Princeton gegen das der Universität Dartmouth absolvierte. Student*innen beider Universitäten gaben die Ereignisse des Spieles derart unterschiedlich wieder, dass die Autoren des Artikels interpretierten, es kann nicht von einem Footballspiel gesprochen werden, sondern von vielen verschiedenen Spielen. Das Spiel als solches existiert nicht! Die Zuschauer*innen geben gewissen Ereignissen auf dem Spielfeld aktiv eine Bedeutung, anderen nicht. Die nicht-relevanten Elemente finden keinen Weg in die Wahrnehmung und werden aussortiert. Ein ganz normaler Vorgang der menschlichen Wahrnehmung und für den Alltag höchst brauchbar. Es wäre unglaublich anstrengend und nicht zielführend, Phänomene wie die Beziehung zu vertrauten Personen ständig aus einer Metaperspektive zu betrachten. Andererseits sollten wir nicht der bekannten Weisheit zum Opfer fallen und Dinge erst schätzen, wenn sie verloren gehen.
Die Frage nach Objektivität und Wahrnehmung ist für uns als Coaches von entscheidender Bedeutung. Wir geben konkrete Handlungsanweisungen und stehen in einem Verantwortungsbereich. Dabei stehen gerade professionelle Coaches immer wieder vor einem Dilemma: Wie sehr ist es nötig und vertretbar Komplexität zu reduzieren und dabei dennoch nach bestem Wissen und Gewissen zu handeln?
Genialität ist simpel – oder eben doch nicht?


Ein offener Geist
Wir sind manchmal verblüfft, wie sehr Personen an ihrem Weltbild anhaften. Extreme Formen davon sind verschwörungstheoretische Inhalte und esoterische Heilanwendungen. Dabei werden angebliche alternative Deutungen genau wegen ihres alternativen Charakters als erfahrungsoffen charakterisiert. Das ist allerdings eine unzulässige Verknüpfung. Offenheit zeichnet sich nicht durch Andersartigkeit aus, sondern durch das Zulassen von Unsicherheit und Zweifel.


Persönliche Werte als Orientierung
Die Unterscheidung zwischen Weltbildorientierung und Werteorientierung ist von zentraler Bedeutung. Kant unterscheidet mit zwei seiner vier Fragen diesen Umstand: „Was kann ich wissen?“ und „Was soll ich tun?“. Für unser alltägliches Handeln ist die zweite Frage von zentraler Bedeutung. Unsere Werte geben uns die Orientierung, um das Erfahrene handlungsorientiert statt erkenntnisorientiert einzuordnen.
Wie die Welt ist, bleibt für uns verborgen. Wie wir aber in Ihr handeln, können wir jedoch kontrollieren. Wo Unsicherheit und Angst vermieden werden, findet keine neue Erfahrung statt und damit keine Veränderung.


Was müsste passieren, damit ich meine Meinung zu X ändere?
Diese Frage kann ein mächtiges Werkzeug gegen die eigene Verblendung sein. Aber nur, wenn sie gewissenhaft und ehrlich bearbeitet wird. Es ist auch sicher keine Frage, die final beantwortet werden sollte – sie ist ein kontinuierlicher Leitfaden.
Sie ist die zentrale Frage, mit der nicht nur das Thema an sich in den Fokus rückt, sondern auch unsere eigene Identität und unser Denken.
Diese Frage mussten sich in der Vergangenheit bereits viele Menschen stellen. Häufig war es wohl leider so, dass die Meinungen eher mit einer jüngeren Generation wegbrachen als innerhalb einer Person…

Was würde mich davon überzeugen, dass nicht die Erde das Zentrum ist, sondern die Sonne?
Was würde mich davon überzeugen, dass Aderlass keine gute Therapiemethode ist?
Was müsste passieren, damit ich Schizophrenie als Erkrankung und nicht als Wirkung eines Dämons anerkenne?
Was müsste passieren, damit ich glaube, dass Homosexualität eine “normale” Variation sexueller Orientierung ist?

Auch heute noch müssen wir uns immer wieder besinnen und unseren Standpunkt auskundschaften. Für uns bei Embodymate stellt sich beispielsweise nicht nur die Frage, wie wir die Embodiment-Theorie anerkannter machen und die klinische Relevanz der Theorie hervorheben. Wir müssen uns auch und vor allem fragen:

Was müsste passieren, damit wir die Embodiment-Theorie ablegen und zum Beispiel eine neurozentrierte Theorie annehmen?

Suchen wir bei unserer internen Forschung also nach Belegen für unsere Meinung oder bilden wir uns unsere Meinung nach den Belegen, die existieren?


Warum ist das eigentlich so schwierig?
Die hier beispielhaft angeführten Fragen stellen eine Herausforderung dar, weil sie unser persönliches Weltbild angreifen. Werden sie nicht mit voller Absicht und klarer Intention angegangen, ist das Experiment zum Scheitern verurteilt.
Wer seine Meinung ändert, wird angreifbar. Der eigene Beruf oder sogar enge Freundschaften können von diesen Weltbildern abhängen. Möglicherweise hat man in der Vergangenheit viel Zeit und Energie dafür aufgewendet, die eigene Meinung aufzubauen und zu vertreten.
Als Sportwissenschafter (Peter) und Psychotherapeut (Christoph) haben wir uns gewisser Ideen verschieben. Es ist uns ein leichtes einen Bericht zu lesen, der eine pharmakologische Therapie bei Depression als wirksamer zeigt als aktive Therapieformen und in dem Bericht irgendein Schlupfloch zu finden, um unser Weltbild nicht zu beschädigen. Der Bericht wurde dann gekauft; die Studienergebnisse spiegeln die Realität nicht wider; die Stichprobe war schlecht gewählt oder zu klein oder nicht auf die richtige Art randomisiert; die Studiendauer war zu kurz; es wurden zu viele Personen ausgeschlossen; und so weiter… Natürlich, das sind doch triftige Gründe, ein Studienergebnis abzulehnen, oder?
Das Anhaften am eigenen Weltbild ist eine evolvierte, sinnvolle Heuristik, die uns vor der Missgunst unserer Ingroup schützt und uns eine stabile Persönlichkeit vorgaukelt. Nur so können wir in einer komplexen Welt überhaupt funktionieren. In einigen Bereichen unseres Wirkens sollten wir uns jedoch um den Einriss eines Weltbildes kümmern, uns selbst einer Art Test unterziehen. Antifragile Theorien werden bestehen bleiben und gestärkt hervorgehen. Die anderen müssen weichen, damit wir uns weiterentwickeln.
Welches Weltbild möchtest du versuchen zum Einsturz zu bringen?

title: Ignorantia
text:
Knowledge is power, and data is the most precious currency of our times. We are trying to gather more information, and it has never been as easy to fact-check someone immediately. Knowledge is now more democratized and, to an extent, independent of education. Everything we need to know is at the tip of our thumbs. This raises a question that concerns everyone: What do we need to know?
This question should be chewed on properly. It’s not just opening up a cynical or nihilistic perspective on learning. It rather questions our relationship to knowing and the unknown. When we think of our deepest discussions or our sparkling curiosity, we find that they are seldom driven by something we know and agree on. It’s the wonders and mysteries that let us look up at the stars, have long conversations, or sudden creative insights. Firestein describes ignorance as the ingredient that drives science. The same can be said about every child that asks Why for the hundredth time (Firestein 2012).
I believe that if we stay on the route we are on and ask the data-ferry in our pockets for the factual answer the moment we are ignorant, we rob ourselves of the most fascinating moments and deepest insights. That is more than just the argument that we unlearn problem-solving or outsource our memory. Allegedly, the ancient Egyptians figured that writing would diminish their ability to memorize. But there are two sides to that story. Freeing the mind of one task opens the door to other tasks. Writing may have affected our working memory negatively, but it also became a powerful “psychotechnology” (Vervaeke), accelerating progress and insights in other domains. Something similar might happen with our accomplishments with silicon brains. But I argue that killing our ignorance is different, because it is not the development of skills alone that dies. What is endangered is the experience of the search itself.
Zen Koans are the ultimate ignorance test. What is the sound of one hand clapping? Does the dog have Buddha nature? Who am I? Students of Zen Buddhism sometimes sit with these kinds of “riddles” for many days or even months without knowing the answer. They are regularly interviewed by their teacher, but seldom is there a single correct answer to give. It is about the quest itself and everything that comes with it. It’s about looking at the question from every direction; turning it around in one’s mind; spitting it out and chewing it again. It’s about the surprise when an insight comes out of nowhere during moments when we stop clinging - in the shower or during a walk. It’s also about the frustration when the answer does not suffice and how one copes with that.
Ignorance and the unknown are the invitation to a Koan and the spice of life. Not engaging in the ignorance is not the nihilistic answer to what we need to know. It is the denial of the Koan. Whether the liberation of fast information is a farce or a genuine blessing is still to be discovered. But for now, we should reframe the question what we need to know.





References

Firestein, Stuart. 2012. Ignorance: How It Drives Science. Oxford University Press.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text: Last semester, I had the privilege of teaching the course Fitness and Lifestyle at the University of Vienna. Twenty sports and human movement science students attended the course and worked on their teaching and coaching skills in different class settings. Students applied best-practice exercise science to different populations and came up with creative solutions to keep it fun and engaging. During the semester, we collected several insights that I will share in this post. We realized the strength of good organization, worked on guiding the group’s energy, and polished our coaching skills. Our thinking was guided by one overarching question: “Who is in charge?”

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
section: Have a detailed plan but stay flexible
text:
Have a detailed plan but stay flexible
We tend to underestimate the time we need for organization and set-up. Create a fixed schedule for each organizational element, set-up, exercise, and discussions. Plan an extra 20% time for the structural tasks of a class, like preparing the exercises or organizing the group.
There is always something that does not work as planned. When you need special equipment or depend on weather conditions, make sure you have a plan B. At least have a general idea of what to do if that specific equipment is unavailable or broken. This will make it so much easier to stay calm and guide the trainees through an alternative.
What are your non-negotiables? No matter how good your plan is, sometimes you run short on time, or you have another fifteen minutes to fill. Have something up your sleeve for both instances. Check your structure and decide upfront which elements you need and which you could leave out if necessary. Have one more game or exercise to pull out for the end. Make this additional exercise as easy to implement as possible. I would go for a variation of an exercise that you already have in class. Another solution is to combine two prior elements into a series or a complex, which would be a good solution if you focus on motor learning. Depending on the class structure, allowing trainees to experiment with any element they liked during class is also a valuable approach, fostering self-efficacy.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Order is your friend
Sports and training can be chaotic, which is generally a good thing. Chaos keeps us alert and creative. That is why good games always induce some form of chaos. Your job as the trainer is to keep the chaos where it belongs. It cannot spill over into the structure and organization of the class. Keeping everything cleaned up is the most important safety rule in many training scenarios - especially when you are working with older adults or children. Equipment that is not in use immediately comes back where it belongs. You can adopt a very loose, easygoing leadership style if that is your thing. Nevertheless, try to get everyone’s buy-in for keeping the movement space clean and tidy. This can improve safety, responsibility, and group coherence!

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Explain effectively
Becoming a good communicator is a key skill in any coaching or training scenario. Have you ever wondered about the announcements on the underground? They always give you the reason for the delay, even if it is just a standard sentence without any actual content: “Due to technical failure, there is currently no service between Schottentor and Wien Mitte.” This does not explain much. But it feels more reasonable to us passengers than just saying there is no train coming. When you explain an exercise, you can use a similar idea.
First, bring up the Why. Give your trainees one brief reason why this particular game or exercise is important.
Second, the announcement is short. Most coaches talk too much! Maybe they lack precise language (at least I sometimes do). Another reason is an overemphasis on details. Find the minimal valuable information your trainees need! For structured exercises, this includes the direct movement goal or intent (“Push the bar towards the ceiling”; “Land with both feet on the yellow line and find your balance for 3 seconds before stepping down.”) and one qualitative criterion, if needed (“Keep your knees locked the whole time”; “Land as silently as a cat.”). For games, the minimal valuable information consists of the task (“Pass the ball without dropping it to the floor”), winning conditions (“Your team wins if you pass it ten times before the other team does so.”), the rule constraints (“No player can catch the ball twice in a row. So when A passes to B, B cannot pass back to A directly.”) and the temporo-spatial constraints (“You have to stay within this area of the room and the game stops whenever one team reaches the win condition.”). For the first round, adding anything else is overkill. Let your trainees practice/play and add further conditions or qualitative criteria 1 for the second set/round.
When working with minimal valuable information, you risk having too little control. Some trainees will explore solutions you did not intend to. It seems like they are breaking the rules - are they? Maybe try reframing this as being creative! Let them explore the movement space and introduce further rules or cues if necessary. Oftentimes the group can help you with that. Remember that you gave them the Why. So they may be able to find the How - which means you acted as a coach and not merely as an instructor.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Target meaning and activation first
The Why I emphasized earlier is an important element for each class and each individual exercise. As a coach, you often work with additional invisible agendas too. Each element has a meaning that you may explicitly share with the class (“We do this so you get better at catching yourself before a fall.”) and maybe others that you don’t (cooperation, social engagement, fun, …). You may not be able to pick the one meaning that best suits all your trainees all the time. So, if you have the chance, you can also invite them to find their meaning. For example, you can show an exercise and briefly explain the targeted muscular area before asking the group where in their lives or in their sport they might need this movement.
Motivation, meaning, and activation are highly interconnected. Activation includes up- and down-regulation of psycho-physiological arousal. Effective exercise and training must be somewhat demanding. However, relaxation and recovery are as essential for long-term performance and health.
Having meaning in place will partly take care of activation and motivation. But you can still directly influence the group’s energy level explicitly or implicitly. Explicit ways to influence activation include games, drills, and direct manipulations such as breathing or awareness exercises. Implicit ways to influence activation include the way you talk and move and the environment you are in. Use all of them to create an intended flow of energy. Typically, you want to raise the activation during the warm-up, peak for some of the non-negotiable elements of the class, and down-regulate at the end.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Explicit manipulation of activation
A wonderful way to get the group going is fast-paced, interactive games. Tasks with direct performance feedback work well. This category includes coordinative exercises that are difficult enough so people fail if they don’t focus. Competitive elements can be included. However, watch the group’s response (especially from the losing side).
Relaxation techniques have been a major topic in our seminar. But don’t throw them at your trainees unprepared and expect immediate effects. This would be like training the squat once and checking your legs to see if you have grown some muscle. Use relaxation techniques in concert with the general training principles. Incorporate them regularly and teach them systematically. Start in a beginner-friendly environment with little distraction. Later you can change the position (seated instead of lying down), the level of distraction (reduce guidance, change the environment), or the timing (create relaxation in an instant instead of guiding through a 20min full-body relaxation exercise). But all of this has to be learned!

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Implicit manipulation of activation
I sometimes find myself showing an exercise to my trainees without the intention and preparation I expect from them. This often leads to similarly loose preparation when they perform the movement. Whenever I do the opposite and, for example, show the whole set-up of a deadlift as if I would go for a demanding working set even with an empty bar, the trainees also tend to approach the exercise with a similar focus and intention. Whatever energy you express during the class may be taken up by the trainees. The way you coach, your posture, voice, and movement - all are important. You can use these as tools to guide the trainees. Speak slowly and calmly during cool-downs, or louder and energetically when you want to push the class. Think about your position in the room and how you walk or demonstrate a movement.
The environment - music, lighting, people watching - can make a difference too. I found dance teachers, but also some yoga teachers, to be the masters of this. The music is not a background element but systematically supports the activity and guides through the class. Some additional caveats should be given here: You cannot serve every music taste. Just make sure not to violate everyone’s eardrums and check your group’s overall response. Think about attention and focus when playing music. If you want to avoid distraction 2, limit vocals and fast-changing structure and style within a song. Both pull attention away from the movement or your coaching. Even if you, yourself, can focus while playing heavy metal, your trainees might not.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Outsource time and timing
The more organizational work you outsource, the more you can focus on coaching, connecting to the trainees, and being fully present and engaged. During interval training, time is an essential part of loading parameters. For those classes, I use the Tabata Timer app on my phone (Android, Apple). If the time is not an integral part of the exercise, set fixed milestones in your class. For example, if you want to have fifteen minutes for a cool down and your class ends at 19:00, write down the actual time (18:45) next to the exercise in your notes or set an alarm on your watch. This way you cannot miss the last element.
The coach alone keeps time! If you master the timing of the class so there is no rushing through the last exercises or losing track of time, you will find that you and the trainees feel secure and relaxed - prerequisites for an engaging exercise session.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Environment - Person - Task
The immediate environment in which the movement takes place gives rise to certain movement options. The surface, the lighting, and the openness of space change movement affordances and constraints, as well as perception during a game. These changes affect motor learning, performance, and injury risk. Potentially, they even drive biological adaptations. In addition, there is a broader perspective to the effects of the environment.
The environment changes how you can coach, communicate, and how the session may feel. When deciding where to locate the training session, consider factors like sun exposure and air quality. Choosing the right environment depends on the group you are working with. While you will not be concerned about the risk of falling on uneven or changing surfaces with children 3, you may choose safety with a group of older adults. At the same time, you may consider clear spatial restrictions when working with children to keep them closer together and allow effective coaching.  Social exposure might be another key factor. Some of your trainees might not enjoy training in public. Think about this especially when working with vulnerable groups.
During the seminar, we also discussed the potential effects of Green exercise. Research on mental health and well-being suggests that exposure to natural environments during exercise is superior to indoor or urban exercise interventions. A recent meta-analysis shows benefits on symptoms of anxiety, depression, and distress in clinical and healthy populations (Liang et al. 2026). It is not fully understood how Green exercise improves mental health and well-being, and there was some controversy about the methodological limitations of the research (Laezza et al. 2024). Nevertheless, the research, including studies on green spaces and health (e.g., Kondo et al. 2018), should be considered by coaches. If you can, get outside!

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Check your own energy
Good trainers or coaches constantly check their group’s well-being and emotional state. They care about how the people in their class are feeling. It also gives constant feedback on how to adjust the exercises, the setting, or when to address certain aspects. Great coaches not only look at their group’s energy, but also check in with themselves. This is harder during a focused and engaging coaching session. But it can be crucial. Handle yourself with as much care as you do your athletes. Your trainees may need some rest or a water break - so do you! You want them to better understand their fatigue and performance by implementing self-ratings - so can you.
When you plan your training session, find one or two slots during which you can check in with yourself. This may not take longer than two to three breaths or briefly closing the eyes. This is probably not the right time for a full reflection on how everything is going. But at least you can center yourself, maybe remember what your intention for the class was or just realize how much joy this work may bring you.
Sometimes you may get tired, confuse the order of the planned exercises, or have to think about scenarios that come up during a game. Don’t worry - every coach has been there! Maybe this is the right moment for a water break or a quick peer-coaching (see below). Take the 2-3 minutes to step back, check your plan, breathe and get back to work.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Concrete, honest feedback
If you have managed most of the points made so far, you are well prepared. You have freed some mental capacity to engage with your group and can focus on effective coaching. Besides motivational support, many trainees want individualized technical feedback. If the exercises and games are well designed, trainees should get immediate feedback on the outcome (i.e., knowledge of outcome). Your job is to give information on their performance (knowledge of performance). Try to be direct and honest when providing feedback. A general “You are doing great!” to the group does not cut it. If you don’t mean it and give no explanation of what exactly they are doing great, it will sound like an empty phrase - which it is. Figure out what is working well and where the person can improve. Also, remember that on the one hand, people may expect a fair amount of direct coaching instructions (“keep the elbow at 90 degrees!”). On the other hand, there is a risk of overcoaching (Janz 2009). So, step back and identify what is really necessary and important before providing your opinion. Even better, create a culture in which trainees can ask for feedback when they think they need it.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Peer-coaching - Everyone is a coach
Compared to one-on-one coaching, groups have several advantages in terms of motor learning and motivation. Instead of seeing groups as having one coach for twenty athletes, we can also view it as having twenty coaches for each trainee. For some parts, this happens automatically. Trainees can watch each other during movements and learn effective and ineffective solutions. Whenever you give direct feedback to one person, others may pick that up too and can learn without making the same mistake themselves. You can also have trainees show a new exercise while you explain it instead of showing it yourself. This all falls under the realm of model-based learning and is highly effective because, in this case, the model is more relatable than the coach. For example, it might give an older person a better perspective of the movement if they see it done by another older person instead of their fit, 25-year-old trainer (more on this here).
You can also try the method of peer-coaching, for example when two trainees pair up to perform an exercise in turns. Now the resting person steps into the role of a coach and gives the working trainee feedback on their form. This not only helps the exercising person. Also, the peer-coach will get a better understanding of the movement by observation, forming explicit knowledge and transforming it into language. In the long run, you should try to improve your athlete’s coaching skills, which will make this method even more effective. Start by giving them checklists for movement quality, add some coaching “rules” like: Always watch from at least two different angles; If the movement is not immediately dangerous, wait till after the movement to give advice; Only correct one thing at a time; Show more - talk less; etc.
With time, peer-coaching will gain momentum, and you can foster an environment of growth and learning. You may also find some hidden strengths when someone who may not be the best athlete turns out to be a valuable coach.

title: Teaching health-related fitness groups
text:
Who is in charge?
Guiding a group of diverse people through an exercise program or creating engaging and fruitful games that are open to everyone is science and art. If you can manage to invoke the joy of moving alone, together with (cooperative) and against (competitive) others while improving people’s fitness, you are doing something powerful and important. Take a step back from time to time to reflect on whom you are doing this for and who is at the center of every action. You may be the coach, and maybe you see yourself as a leader or manager. But ultimately you are part of the group and the class you facilitate. You can all share the experience, the decisions, and the power of moving. Find out which elements of a class should be dictated by you and which elements may be better distributed. You have the bird’s-eye view, but your trainees feel the movement and what it does to them.
Each of the provided points in this article has elements that are centered around the coach and others that are centered around the trainee. These are no perfect solutions but invitations to reflect. Who is it for? Who has the critical information? Who can decide? Who may need support? Coaching is about people’s interactions.

title: Outside Academia
text:
As I have written on the front page, science and scholarship are activities of leisure. However, scientists must also live on something. Many of the known scientists of the past lived from family wealth. They did the experiments and observations out of curiosity, leisure, fame, glory, or to serve god. Nowadays, things are different. While academic researchers do enjoy prestige in some respects, the financial rewards are relatively limited. This is especially true concerning extensive education, high working hours, and the low probability of reaching the top of the food chain, which mostly means securing tenure. For many, an alternative route is entering the industry. This is a more realistic route for some research areas than others and nearly impossible for some.



academia vs industry


Sometimes, there is some middle ground. Some scientists hit the “jackpot” and do both. They enjoy the freedom of academia and, as a related sideshow, they work in the private sector. For health and performance-related fields (the ones that I am most interested in) like sports and exercise science, psychology, and nutrition, this might involve giving seminars, selling books, working with supplement companies, or leveraging one’s research ideas into other profitable products.
This is more common than one might think. Probably, some big names come to your mind that do exactly that. So, in essence, they are selling the expertise they have carved out over years or decades of work. Fair thing, right? Let me make this clear: Some independent scientists directly use the leverage they gain to fund their research with good intentions. Some claim that their breakthroughs would not have been possible in the traditional way because nobody believed in their work and they couldn’t get funding.
Researchers are faulty human beings. Regardless of whether they are funded by a national funding agency or their own company - driven by personal beliefs and the urge to be right. We are invested in our ideas and hypotheses. I do not know if everybody is, but I certainly am1. I do not believe that being invested in an idea is completely avoidable. But caution is advisable if scientists sell products (or knowledge) related to their research. It might sound like a good thing if popular Stanford professors claim that their podcast is independent of their role as researchers, but I am not convinced that can be true. Not only because they (probably) have no chance, but being the same person!
Sure, “research is me-search” and personal investment might come with higher motivation, drive and creativity. This makes the objective work vulnerable and contaminates your role as a researcher. Another profession has known about that for hundreds of years. That might be why, in many traditions, priests are not allowed to have a family or sex. That’s how they stay independent and hard to bribe (in theory).


Making research available to the public is a significant component of modern science and is incentivized and with good reason. We want educated and responsible citizens!
BUT WHY SELL IT??? That’s the whole point.
We want people - all people - to get access to the knowledge base. We are dissatisfied with the influence of large publishing houses. However, it is hard to change that in the case of peer-reviewed articles without risking one’s career. We talk about the FAIR principles within the ivory tower of science. But why not expand these principles beyond that?
We can and should leverage all those problems into unrestricted publications, such as blogs or free online books.
Publish your teaching openly: I myself started putting one of my undergraduate seminars into written form and publishing it on Bookdown2. This makes my seminar not only more transparent for students but also allows the information to be updated on a regular basis. Even after finishing the course, students can easily access the information. One could argue that you no longer need to attend the seminar, as all the information is accessible for free on the internet. But in my opinion, that is the case anyway. I can not tell our students any exercise training secrets anyway. Nobody should go to university for that explicit, teachable information anymore. We passed that point a long time ago! The good news is that we can focus on experimental learning and carve out competencies3!
Writing blog posts about your research: Traditional scientific journal articles can only withstand so much information. The general consensus in many fields is not to spoil the reader with too much personal experience, different challenges during various phases of the project. I think even in pre-prints and other publishing formats that are more researcher-centered, we hold on to the traditional writing style, like using passive voice as if everything was executed by an emotionless and error-free research robot. In reality, there is often some kind of thinking, tweaking, rethinking, and frustration involved. Sharing those things might improve project science. Writing those protocols in a personal way might not only help you resolve some of the project-related issues but also make the work of the grad student working on a similar project at another university easier. Humanizing our daily work by writing about it is also a way to make science and scientists more relatable for people outside of academia. We have a huge problem of trust in science. Simply informing people on “how reality works” does not do the trick to improve that. Playing with open cards might!
But being relatable is also something we should work for within Team Science. Seeing that all science (not only my project) is messy. There are struggles that go beyond low statistical power and deadlines. I personally would love to see more unrestricted writing from scientists. I would love to see less profit-oriented side gigs and more real content - raw, personal, and messy

title: A discussion of Training
text: Most of my (formal and informal) education falls into the realm of training science. So, I want to start right there and give an introduction to what I mean by training. In this blog post, I wrestle with the concept of training, learning, practice, and development. This is not my final thought on this topic. Don’t be surprised to end up with more questions than answers after reading it. Good food for thought has to get chewed on - a lot.

title: A discussion of Training
text:
Three sites of adaptations:
It is helpful to categorize adaptations. This helps in forming theory, explanations, and predictions, which are necessary for higher-order processing and control. I differentiate three levels of adaptation: Biological capacities, function, and structures. An example of a capacity is the ability to run a marathon or carry groceries. Other examples are improved reading or writing speed or the ability to keep attention on the breath. Capacities manifest as the observable and meaningful outcomes and can, in theory, be explained by function and structure. The downside is that capacities are never directly measurable. The expression of capacities as performance depends on the environment, task, and other personal factors. As an example, you cannot know your “true” aerobic endurance capacity because it depends on the event, the temperature, your motivation, food intake, and a million other aspects. Similar arguments might be made for the other levels of adaptation, but it is most dominant for capacity. The second level, biological function, refers to the ability to change internal states. Good examples are changes in heart rate or blood glucose levels during different demanding situations. In general, function is observable as energy flux. This is a more direct operationalization than capacity but less meaningful in relation to performance and goal-directed behavior. The third, and most fundamental level, adaptations in biological structures. These are changes in tissue size, organization, or molecular composition, like increased muscle volume, number of red blood cells, or changes in collagen types. Major chronic changes in biological structure are often slow or require repeated, high demands relative to capacity. At the same time, transient micro changes to biological structure are always happening and are the basis for adaptations in function and capacity. In summary, adaptations to capacities are often the aim of a training process. They are not directly measurable, and meaningful changes can take place within seconds. From the individual’s perspective, capacities are determined by function and structure. Biological function can be described as the ability to transform energy. In contrast to capacity, function is directly observable as the rate of change. Structure is the most fundamental aspect. It is the time-invariant state of the biological system. While it can change rapidly, on a macro level, structure is relatively stable. Training is goal-oriented. The goal can be defined on any level of adaptation. What is then needed is a mechanistic reason or explanation that links the demands to the intended adaptations. If training is always goal-oriented, as standard in contemporary textbooks, someone MUST have a conscious, explicit explanation and prediction model of what works. This means that there is no “training by chance”. Adaptations to physical activity that are not led by goal-oriented reasoning cannot be considered training. They are something else. This even makes the word cross-training effects a misnomer. If you train to get stronger in lifting weights and after a couple of weeks you realize you have become a better runner, this cannot be a training effect.

title: A discussion of Training
text:
Training vs Learning and Development
Learning is a very similar process of long-term adaptations. As with training, learning happens through the interplay of environmental demands and the person. For learning, only changes that occur within the person are relevant (not of the task or the environment). Besides the similarities, the two distinctions between learning and training are (1) the need for prior experience and (2) the goal-orientation and long-term planning in training. (1) Learning does not need prior experience. If you cannot ride a snowboard yet and you start sliding (and falling) down a hill, you are learning. When you start following a scheduled structure to improve your snowboarding skills, you are training. At first, this sounds like a bulletproof difference. However, it’s hard to see where prior experience comes into play and where learning ends and training starts. (2) Learning and training differ in the need for higher-order processing (model B). Learning does not necessarily include a conscious plan. You can learn for an exam (goal-oriented and structured), but you can also unconsciously learn to avoid social gatherings (not goal-oriented, unstructured). In this scenario, learning can even happen within a very short timeframe. Sometimes it only needs one exposure to permanently learn something. Training never happens within one session. It always needs regular exposure to demands over a longer period. There is another difference that might come to mind. Learning could be defined as adaptations that solely happen in the central nervous system (CNS). I don’t think this is a helpful distinction when it comes to the whole organism. When learning to walk or to play the piano, adaptations will span throughout other systems, especially the musculoskeletal. Motor performance is not entirely regulated by the CNS but includes self-organizing properties of muscles. Further, efficient walking does need certain bone configurations and architecture of the foot. These are not automatic, developmental changes (see below) but only happen through practicing walking. Transient adaptations are typically not considered learning. This is something that bites many coaches when they confuse improvements during a session with long-term learning. In reality, these two live in an orthogonal space (see here). Development is a close relative of learning. It happens independently of environmental demands. As long as the right prerequisites are given, development happens automatically. It often follows a non-linear timeline. Within a person, learning and development are indistinguishable. This gives rise to misinterpretations and false attributions. For example, some young athletes are called talents but are just further in their development. They later end up being merely average after the others catch up. Other times, coaches falsely earn credit for improving capacities while developmental spurts occur. This is similar to a medical intervention, whose effects cannot be distinguished from the normal “development” of the pathology. Coaches and teachers must be aware of this trap and read developmental patterns in their trainees as well as possible. Otherwise, wrong interventions will lead to wrong conclusions, and performance will stagnate, or trainees will drop out or get injured. In summary, learning involves long-term changes in behaviors or expressing completely new behaviors independent of goal-orientation. Training is a process of improving already existing patterns. The pattern of behavior was already learned. So maybe training should be defined as a subcategory of learning. One more caveat to the difference between training and learning is based on higher-order processing. The predetermined goal that is inherent in training does not have to be “known” to the organism performing the training. A rat or a pigeon can be trained without it understanding the training process. The animal is then learning, but the person who is the teacher is training it. Before physiological adaptation was the popular underpinning of related scientific fields, training principles were influenced by psychology. During that time, behaviorism was the proper way to frame human learning 1 (Krüger 2006). Training principles for a human (or a rat, as the most influential scientists of that time didn’t see much of a difference) were radically different from today’s viewpoint. A person could be trained by “conditioning” without the person being aware of it. Consciousness was not important for that framework. The scientist would play god and transform the person/animal into “whatever they like”2. Somebody still has to be aware, but not necessarily the trainee. A religious person believing in a greater plan that unfolds might call any learning process also training. But for the rest of us, there is a difference.
While training focuses on the planning and structuring of goal-directed behavior, learning focuses on the adaptations that happen.

title: A discussion of Training
text:
Practice
Writing this, I realized that I missed out on the concept of practice, which is funny as I like this word a lot (link blog post to practice). In sports, art, and music, as well as in spirituality, practice is quite often used to describe regular behavior. What makes it different from training is the focus on the skill component or the functional capacity (highest level of adaptations) and, with it, neurocentered adaptations. It’s in the realm of structured and goal-oriented learning. But it can also mean something different. A practice can also be something that is indifferent to goal-orientation and improvement. It can have an athletic component and give meaning through the behavior itself. This is a definition that can be found in spirituality but can certainly be adopted for other kinds of behavior. Physical practices can have their meaning in the act of doing them.
We saw training as the planning and structuring, learning as the behavioral adaptations, and practice as the repeated behavior itself.

title: A discussion of Training
text:
Measure and manage
This all leads us back to the problem of tracking expected and unexpected changes in capacity, function, and structure. Typically, we only measure the outcome we previously specified as important. There are more general ways to measure any changes in the categories previously defined. This data-mining approach to tracking changes seems to come up naturally in practitioners. But these changes are not training-induced changes for reasons outlined above. The definition of training seems to be very much in line with a deductive, hypothesis-driven way of doing science. In practice, we do not handle it like that and mix it up with inductive methods and post hoc reasoning. I think this is actually a good thing. Historically, training principles can be understood from an inductive perspective. We built our ideas on how to train by observing changes time and time again. This blog post ended up as a struggle. I realized that many of the conventions about what training ought to be don’t hold up against how we use the word as practitioners. There is also no hard wall between learning, practice, and training. To progress our understanding of guided adaptations that improve health and performance, we should keep wrestling with these concepts until we understand their meaning, how to observe them, and how to induce them.
